title: 'Good suffering': Yliniemi wins Sasquatch Run Last One Standing with 24-hour, 100-mile performance
excerpt: The Sasquatch Trail Run single-loop and Last One Standing ultramarathon races on Saturday, Sept. 26, saw double the registrants compared to last year.
content:
DETROIT LAKES — Just before 10 a.m. Sunday, Sept. 27, fog settled over Detroit Mountain as Laurie Yliniemi, her calves and shoes coated in mud, jogged up the tubing hill through thick, tacky muck left by a full day of rain Saturday.

When she reached the top, Yliniemi of Detroit Lakes had run for 24 hours and nearly 100 miles to win the Sasquatch Run Last One Standing race, a backyard-style ultramarathon.

She said her first thoughts at the finish went to the friends and family who were there. She came to the race with a group of eight, about a month after running the Leadville Trail 100 Run, an ultramarathon in Leadville, Colorado.

"I love challenging others; I love challenging myself," she said. "This is a great way to do it."

The Sasquatch Run trail races, put on in part by Project 412, returned to Detroit Mountain last year after a three-year hiatus. As in 2025, runners could sign up for a single 4.16-mile trail loop or for the Last One Standing race. In that race, participants must complete the loop at the top of every hour until only one person remains.

Registration nearly doubled from last year, with about 60 runners in each race.

"Everyone's in good spirits," race director James Botnen said Saturday morning. "They know it's an adventure, and we're just excited to see how long this day lasts."

Before the start, last year's winner, Jonathan Peabody of Fargo, sat beneath a blue tent stocked with totes of food and supplies, a setup much like the others around him. He was nursing an injured knee this year, but the sense of fun he showed last year was back.

"I like this race a lot," he said. "I think it's easier on me than doing, like, a marathon, where I have to go all out. All you have to do is not stop running."

At 9 p.m. Saturday, the last 12 runners set out on another lap. Many trickled back about 10 minutes before the hour, their headlamps peeking through the woods along the way. Botnen said runners told him the last mile was more like a river.

Botnen and other volunteers gave fist bumps at the end of every lap. One racer said he "died but (he) lived."

"It's good suffering," he told Botnen.

Sunday morning, runner-up Luke Steichen of Fargo sat in a chair beneath his tent after nearly 23 hours of running. His pale, waterlogged feet showed what nearly a full day of rain had done to the trails as his fiancé, Geneva Noland, helped him manage the mud leftover on his calves. When Yliniemi finished, she and Steichen embraced.

"There's something about the ultra community that's really unexplainable," Botnen said. "That's really what's unique about the last one standing concept: You stay together, you help each other through tough times, you rest, and then you get started in the next hour.”

Abby Fostveit is a reporter and staff photographer for the Detroit Lakes Tribune and Perham Focus. Before moving to the area, Fostveit graduated with a degree in journalism and a minor in environmental studies from Butler University in Indianapolis in May 2024, where she also competed on the cross country and track and field teams as a middle-distance runner.
